subject: Civil Engineering
title: Lateral Force Resisting Systems
description: A micro-lesson that makes Lateral Force Resisting Systems usable.

hook.text: Gravity holds buildings up. But earthquakes push sideways — what resists lateral force?

buildup.text: Moment frames use rigid beam-column connections — they flex but hold together.

discovery.text: Braced frames add diagonal steel members — triangles resist lateral loads efficiently.

twist.text: Shear walls are solid panels — concrete or steel — that act like vertical cantilever beams.

climax.text: Most tall buildings combine systems — shear core with perimeter moment frames.

punchline.text: Earthquakes attack from the side. Every building needs a system to push back.

quiz.question: How do braced frames resist lateral earthquake forces?
options: They use heavy concrete weights at the top to counterbalance swaying
Diagonal steel members form triangles that efficiently resist sideways loads
They disconnect from the foundation to allow free movement

details.summary: Lateral force resisting systems are the structural elements designed to resist horizontal earthquake and wind forces. The three primary systems are moment frames that resist forces through rigid beam-column connections, braced frames that use diagonal members in tension and compression.
details.whyItMatters: The choice of lateral system determines a building's stiffness, ductility, and cost. It is the most fundamental decision in the structural design of any building in an earthquake zone.
takeaways: Moment frames allow open floor plans but are flexible and expensive for tall buildings
Braced frames use diagonal members to create stiff, efficient triangulated systems
Shear walls are extremely stiff and efficient for resisting lateral forces

faq.question: Why are moment frames more flexible than braced frames or shear walls?
faq.answer: Moment frames resist lateral forces through bending in beams and columns at their rigid connections. Bending is inherently a flexible mechanism. Braced frames and shear walls resist forces through axial action in diagonal members or in-plane stiffness, which is much stiffer per unit of material.

faq.question: Can different lateral systems be combined in one building?
faq.answer: Yes. Dual systems combine moment frames with shear walls or braced frames. The shear walls or braces provide stiffness to control drift, while the moment frame provides redundancy if the primary system is damaged. Codes reward this redundancy by allowing lower design forces for dual systems.
